Talk for Writing · Zelda Claw

Toolkit 2:
Rhetorical Questions

Can a question make the reader feel worried?

LESSON 201
Learning intention

To make the reader worried by using rhetorical questions.

Success Criteria

  • Identify a rhetorical question.
  • Write a rhetorical question that makes the reader worried or curious.
  • Choose words that create suspense.
  • Use a question mark (?) correctly.
  • Place my question at an important moment to make the reader wonder what happens next.
LEARNING INTENTION02
Picture prompt · Zelda

Look closely at the cat.

Talk together

  • What can you see?
  • How is Zelda feeling?
  • What might be nearby?
  • What question could Zelda be asking?
Possible questions:
What was it?
Had it seen her?
Could she escape?
HOOK · PICTURE TALK03
What is a rhetorical question?

A question that makes the reader think or worry.

Ordinary question

“What time is it?”

You expect an answer.

Rhetorical question

“Was something watching her?”

The reader does not know the answer yet.

EXPLAIN04
Find it in the model text

Questions from Zelda Claw

“Where could she escape from the rain?”

“What was it?”

“Had it seen her?”

Discuss

  • Which one feels most suspenseful?
  • Why does it make you want to keep reading?
  • Where has the writer placed it?
READ AS A WRITER05
Placement matters
“Had it seen her?”

Why is this question powerful right here?

The danger is close. Zelda may have been spotted. The question pauses the action and makes the reader desperate to know the answer.

WHY IT WORKS06
Teacher modelling

Change a statement into a suspenseful question.

Statement: The creature was getting closer.

Had the creature found her hiding place?

I DO07
Quick check

Which one builds more suspense?

COMPARE AND JUSTIFY08
Support

Question starters and sentence frames

Question starters

Had it...?Was someone...?Could she...?What was...?Would it...?

Sentence frames

His / Her ________ as he / she looked towards the ________.
Had ________ ?
SCAFFOLD09
Shared writing

Use the cat prompt to build a question.

Write together

  1. Choose the dangerous moment.
  2. Start with a question starter.
  3. Add detail that makes the reader worried.
WE DO10
Innovation prompt

Now try a new scene.

Look at the new picture

  • What is happening?
  • How is the dog feeling?
  • Who or what is nearby?
  • What question could the dog be asking?
This follows the same suspense pattern as Zelda Claw — a lone character, bad weather, danger nearby, and uncertainty.
INNOVATION · NEW PROMPT11
Support for the new picture

Use these ideas if you get stuck.

Question starters

  • Had it followed him?
  • Was someone there?
  • Could he escape?
  • What was in the doorway?

Word bank

  • trembled
  • froze
  • glanced
  • flickering
  • shadowy
  • lurking

Sentence frames

  • The dog ________ as he looked towards the doorway.
  • Rain ________ around him.
  • Had ________ ?
SUPPORTED WRITING12
Independent writing

Write a mini suspense scene.

Choose one prompt

Use either the cat picture or the dog picture.

Include

  • 4–6 connected sentences
  • one physical reaction
  • one rhetorical question
  • capital letters, punctuation and neat spelling
YOU DO13
Model example

Here is one possible response.

Rain hammered the alleyway as the little dog froze beneath the flickering lamp. A shadow moved in the doorway behind him. His legs trembled and he glanced over his shoulder. Had something followed him into the lane? He took one slow step backwards.

Find the physical reaction and the rhetorical question.

MODEL EXAMPLE14
Check your work

Editing checklist

  • My question makes the reader worried.
  • I used a question mark correctly.
  • I placed my question at an important moment.
  • I used capital letters.
  • I checked my end punctuation.
  • I checked spelling and neatness.
REVIEW15
Exit ticket

Which is better?

“Was the dog scared?” or “Had something followed him into the lane?”

Explain:

“I chose _____ because it makes the reader _____.”

REFLECT16
